boreholes far from cottages were comparatively low implying that those boreholes received less impact of polluted water. Surrounding agricultural land was a further nutrient source. Boreholes at the edge of the site were noticeably richer (by an order of 10) in nitrate than those at the centre. Pools 11 and 14, closest to the arable agricultural areas to the south and east of the site were consequently much richer in nitrate than any of the others. In winter increased nitrogen concentrations in the pools and boreholes corresponded well with an increase of water level suggesting that fertilizers and manure applied to crops around Brown Moss can get into the pools and boreholes through surface run-off and sub-surface percolation (Berka et al., 2001). Pool 3, situated towards the inner area of Brown Moss, surrounded by woodland, and on the western side where more of the agriculture is pastoral, had lower concentrations of nitrogen. Trees around this pool may help reduce nutrients from external sources since nutrients can be removed through uptake by plants and sediment denitrification based on litter as an organic source (Sondergaard et al., 2005). However, its phosphorus concentrations in contrast were still high and may be derived from local septic tank drainage. The site as a whole suffers onslaught from both of the conventional sources of effluent and diffuse drainage from agriculture with different pools affected by different sources. The patterns of conductivity and alkalinity, however, offer little help in interpretation. Pools 2 and 7 have relatively low values and lie on the west of the site but other westward pools have much higher values. Borehole water shows lower values to the west also but it seems likely that there is an effect Fig. 7 Mean usages of bird (month ha\(^{-1}\)) in pools 3, 6 and 14 ![Bar charts showing mean usages of bird (month ha\(^{-1}\)) in pools 3, 6, and 14, with data for winter, spring, summer, and autumn.](page_320_180_1408_1012.png) of patchiness in the glacial drift overlying the site and that the water supply in some cases is highly localised. We found high concentrations of ammonium nitrogen in pool 6 compared with other pools and this may be a consequence of congregation of waterfowl. We found that dense congregation of waterfowl, mainly Canada geese, raised ammonium concentrations in pool 6 in winter 2004 (Chaichana et al., 2010). Solid wastes excreted by water birds in winter may subsequently affect water chemistry in summer as they decompose. Nutrient budgets for pool 6 showed substantial release of phosphorus and ammonium from the sediments in summer and birds were the major external loading source of phosphorus (Chaichana et al., 2010). This effect is unlikely to extend to other pools as there were much greater species numbers and densities of waterfowl on pool 6 than in the smaller pools 3 and 14. In particular, larger birds such as Canada geese and swans were confined to pool 6 since it has sufficient space for larger birds to fly in and take off. Compared with pool 6, pools 3 and 14, and other pools on the site, are smaller and surrounded by mature trees and this may cause difficulty in landing for such big birds. Supplementary feeding by the public at pool 6 also encourages and attracts more birds of relatively low conservation value such as black headed gulls to colonize and excrete. Sediment chemistry and site history A limitation of the sediment study was that no dating was available but the lengths of the cores suggest that in pool 6, less than a few decades were covered (on the grounds of sedimentation rates in shallow lakes being a few mm per year and 15 cm of sediment being recovered. The sediment sequence for the bog pool (pond 9) appeared complete, reaching underlying glacial clay but its shortness suggests a comparatively recent origin, perhaps only a few centuries or even less, given the highly preservative conditions of acid water. In pool 4 rapid oxidation of organic matter during dry phases may have prevented sediment accumulation (Collinson et al., 1995). Although a clay layer was reached by the corer, it seems unlikely that a gross accumulation of only 33 cm of sediment could have been laid down in the post-glacial period. There are many uncertainties about this site and its soil stratigraphy has not been systematically explored. The smooth glacial clay underlying the bog pool and clay layers underlying other pools imply that Brown Moss may have been formerly a bigger lake or a wetland that has largely terrestrialised. This is consistent with a map of Brown Moss in 1841 showing that there were only two large pools at the site which formerly could have been just one water body. In pool 4, the lake sediments were richer in nutrients and carbonate had started to build up, perhaps washed out from surrounding land or deposited as marl by aquatic plants. In pool 6, the sediments almost certainly only represent the recent history of Brown Moss. We found a monotonic increase in organic matter and calcium carbonate because of marl formation and this corresponded well with increased production as indicated by diatoms. An increased phosphorus content was also observed in the surficial sediments and this may be related to increased nutrient loading. It is likely that septic tank sources and bird contributions have increased in the recent past (Chaichana et al., 2009; Chaichana et al., submitted). Diatoms in all three pools investigated were absent from the sediments just above the clay layer and the lower sediment, respectively, suggesting that earliest conditions of pool development were probably nutrient poor. There were fewer species of diatoms in the sediments in the bog pool than in pools 4 and 6 perhaps because of the acidic conditions, where other, less tolerant species cannot develop, or perhaps owing to lower nutrient loading in this pool. The main species of diatom in the bog pool was the acid indicator species Frustulia rhomboides. In pools 4 and 6, the variety of diatoms was greater than in the bog pool and pools 4 and 6 are more fertile and less acidic. Eunotia spp. were most abundant in pool 4 and the increase in diatoms corresponded well with contents of phosphorus whereas Melosira sp. was most abundant in sediments of pool 6 and is often associated with more nutrient-rich conditions (Crabtree & Round, 1967). The existence of a very small bog in a small site where water conductivities generally indicate much more minerotrophic conditions is of interest. Conductivities of the two pools (2 and 7) closest to the bog are the lowest on the site (around 110 \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1} \)) and there is (Fig. 2; Table 2) a steady increase in conductivity to the east and south where values are three times as high. It is unclear whether this is determined by the pattern of the original glacial deposits or by a residuum of ombrotrophic peat on the west of the site that has been cut away from the east. There is no immediate evidence of such peat, however. Comparative limnology of three contrasted pools As in other aspects, the aquatic plant communities varied greatly even over such a small site. Plants were more diverse, with greater cover, in pool 6 than in the smaller pools 3 and 14. This finding was similar to other studies in that species richness of submerged macrophytes increased markedly with lake size (Amarasinghe & Welcomme, 2002; Bazzanti et al., 2003; Sondergaard et al., 2005) though the size range in these studies was much greater. The most obvious difference was between the comparatively richer pools 3 and 6, which lacked fish and 14 which contained carp and had high chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations. However, chlorophyll \( a \) was just as high in pool 6, though with greater variability. Vulnerability to drying can be discounted because the permanent pool 14 was the least rich in plants. The shallowness may mean that water transparency is of much less importance than in deeper waters (Coops et al., 2003) and that factors such as bird grazing become important in determining differences from year to year and pool to pool. Nonetheless the variety of the flora was low, its composition now unremarkable and its species diversity reduced compared with surveys in the 1960s (Sinker, 1962; Whild, 2007). There has been a major loss of submerged species, including Luronium natans, only one plant of which was seen and a major increase in the introduced Crassula helmsii, which has spread extensively over the site. Fish were probably a key factor regulating zooplankton communities in the pools. Large cladocerans such as Daphnia were most abundant in the fish-free pools 3 and 6 and in contrast, smaller cladocerans such as Bosmina and rotifers were dominant in pool 14, which had fish. Fish preferentially remove large cladocerans, such as Daphnia as they are easily seen and move slowly through the water (Brooks & Dodson, 1965; Moss et al., 1997). Smaller zooplankters such as rotifers in pool 14 tend to increase with fish predation as competition from larger zooplankters is lessened and they are less easily seen by fish (Andersson et al., 1978). Pools 3 and 6 had higher densities of large cladocerans such as Daphnia pulex and this appears to have an adverse effect on populations of rotifers. Large cladocerans may suppress rotifers by competing for food as they are more efficient feeders (Burns, 1969). Also they may mechanically interfere with rotifers by detachment of eggs from ovigerous individuals or sweeping rotifers into the brachial chamber or ingesting and rejecting rotifers in a damaged condition (Brooks & Dodson, 1965; Gilbert & Stemberger, 1985; Gilbert, 1988). With smaller zooplankters, chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations were higher in pool 14 in summer than in pools 3 and 6, with their larger cladocerans. Zooplankton, mainly *Daphnia* often regulate phytoplankton populations and summer grazing pressure keeps the edible algae at a low biomass (Sommer, 1985; Quiblier-Lloberas et al., 1996). Fish may also have structured the macroinvertebrate communities in Pond 14. Presence of fish reduced other invertebrate predators and, in contrast, absence of fish promoted carnivorous invertebrates such as *Chaoborus*. *Chaoborus* larvae were most abundant in pools 3 and 6 without fish but scarcer in pool 14. In other fishless lakes, large predatory invertebrates such as *Chaoborus, Leptodora*, notonectids and other bugs and beetles, may tend to increase in abundance (Nyberg, 1998; Irfanullah & Moss, 2005; Sondergaard et al., 2005). In the three investigated pools, the macroinvertebrate communities were low in taxon richness. Previously they may have been much richer (personal communication, anonymous referee), with Pool 3 sampled in the 1990s having a total of 57 species with an exceptional water beetle assemblage containing six nationally scarce and one Red data Book species. In the present survey, no beetles were recorded. This might be a function of the recent drying out of the site or of more protracted impacts of water reduction, including water availability, to it. Overall, there is evidence that production of the pools has increased (see also Whild, 2007), that nutrient sources are several and affect individual pools to different extents, and that there is substantial variation across the site and between years in water levels and communities. The origins of the pools are obscure. They have probably become smaller as they have filled in and as vegetation has encroached at the edges. Filling in is not necessarily accompanied by eutrophication, as evidenced by the bog pool with its sparse diatom content and highly acidic nature, but the two processes have probably been occurring together in pool 6. Changes in land use and clearance of forest in the catchment area probably influenced these processes. All of these things make management of the site to maintain biodiversity, the general aim of current conservation philosophy in the UK, a difficult task. This site is now greatly damaged due to people feeding birds, and increasing their numbers, septic tank drainage, and intensive agriculture. Strictly the SSSI does not include pool 14, so the damaging effects of carp (King & Hunt, 1967; Roberts et al., 1995; Domaizon & Dévaux, 1999) represent only a potential threat if the fish is illegally stocked elsewhere on the site. The Site is popular with the public for dog walking and casual visits and lies next to a road. A car park is provided. Feeding ducks is a pastime not easily controlled in a country where gardens are replete with bird-feeders and even the bird conservation organizations encourage the practice. Canada geese, which may be major contributors of nutrients to pool 6, can be controlled but this is difficult for they readily move around the small lakes in the area. It is unlikely that the isolated cottages around the site will be connected to mains sewerage in the near future, the exact locations of the diffuse effluents are not known, obviating local treatment by constructed wetlands, and the problems of controlling diffuse nutrient sources from agricultural land remain intractable. The only workable solution would be to establish a substantial buffer zone of semi-natural vegetation around the site, which would mean abandonment of land valuable to its owners for farming. There are stewardship schemes available to encourage this, but take-up by farmers is voluntary and tends to be adopted only when other use of the land becomes uneconomic. This is hardly the case on the fertile soils of the glacial plain where Brown Moss is situated. The site is included in the current Catchment Sensitive Farming initiative of the UK Government. This scheme seeks voluntary reductions in nutrient loss through capital payments, which can include measures to reduce soil erosion and to divert animal wastes, but these are less important at this site than losses of soluble nitrogen to pools that are mostly nitrogen-sensitive because local phosphorus supplies, derived from septic tanks and birds, have greatly increased. A substantial flaw in UK conservation legislation is that boundaries around SSSI do not reflect natural features, but have been determined on the basis of local biodiversity in the past rather than continued ecosystem function. Thus, aquatic sites typically include only the water body and not the catchment area and are generally in poor condition (Carvalho & Moss, 1995; DEFRA, 2009). The EU Water Framework Directive, passed in 2000, requires catchment (river basin) management but is impotent to guarantee this in the absence of strong national legislation as opposed to reliance on voluntary arrangements. Its provisions are not being vigorously pursued (Environment Agency, 2008; Moss, 2008) and small water bodies receive scant attention. We conclude that, apart from small initiatives within the site, such as continual clearance of the invasive aquatic plant, Crassula helmsii (Kirk), which can potentially blanket the pools, there is little that can be practically done to restore the site to a biodiversity that was still high only 50 years ago (Whild, 2007; personal observation, Brian Moss). Average TSS in the study pools varied from 0.01 to 0.05 mg l−1. Pools 14 and 6 had high values of TSS whereas pools 3, 4, 10 and 11 had low TSS values. Nutrient concentrations of all study pools were generally very high with average SRP concentrations, μg l−1 (overall mean values of SRP 444 μg l−1, TP 624 μg l−1, ammonium nitrogen 1,104 μg l−1, nitrate nitrogen 0.02 mg l−1, TN 3 mg l−1). Concentrations of ammonium nitrogen ranged from 66 to 3,680 μg l−1, nitrate from 0.03 to 2.03 mg l−1 and TN from 2.4 to 6.4 mg l−1. Winter and summer values of nutrients in each pool are given in Table 3. Phosphorus tended to increase markedly in summer and nitrate to decrease. Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations ranged from 14 to 140 μg l−1. Bray–Curtis analysis of nutrients (TP and TN) showed that the study pools at Brown Moss can be divided into three groups. The first group (pools 3 and 4) had relatively low nutrient concentrations compared with other pools. Close similarities among pools 6, 7, 10, 11 and 14 were found, with these pools in a second group with high concentrations of nutrients. The last group is composed of pools 1, 2 and 12 with waters that had very high concentrations of nutrients. All pools were hypereutrophic (with TP values greater than 100 μg l−1 and TN values greater than 1,500 μg l−1). TN:TP ratios also suggested that pools 1, 2, 7, 10 and 12 were nitrogen limited with TN:TP ratios by mass lower than 10. In contrast, phosphorus could have been limiting in pool 4 where the TN:TP ratio was greater than 17. TN:TP ratios of pools 3, 6, 11 and 14 were between 10 and 17 suggesting that phosphorus or nitrogen could be limiting. Levels of ground water fluctuated greatly in the boreholes. The lowest and highest levels recorded were 0 and 72 cm (measured from the bottom of the borehole to the groundwater surface) in September 2005 and in May 2006, respectively. Changes in ground water table in boreholes were consistent with level changes in pool 6 and a significant positive correlation between water levels in pool 6 and in boreholes was found (\( r = 0.529, P = 0.016 \)). Average TP concentrations were higher in boreholes 1, 3, 5, 9 and 10 and similarly TN concentrations were high in boreholes 1, 5, 7 and 10. Lower amounts of nutrients were found in boreholes 2, 4, 6 and 8 installed in the inner areas of Brown Moss. Sediment chemistry and site history In the bog pool 9, which has a floating mat of Sphagnum, the sediment layer under the water lens and above the basal clay layer, was approximately 15 cm thick, suggesting low rates of sediment accumulation or a recent origin. The sediment was black at its surface and gradually became brown and gray towards the basal clay layer. pH of the water was 3.8. All variables in the sediments showed a tendency to decrease toward the bottom of the core (Fig. 3). The extent of the sediment layer in pool 4 was about 33 cm, deeper than in the bog pool, but still modest. There was some discontinuity with sharp coincident and upward increases in loss on ignition and total phosphorus at 13 and 23 cm. In pool 6, the sediment was black and contents of water, carbonate and loss on ignition were relatively constant but tending to decrease with depth. pH value of the pool was 7.5. Unmodified basal clay, if present, was not reached and the total sediment depth is unknown. Most diatoms were in the top 10-cm of sediments and numbers of diatoms decreased with increasing depth in all study pools (Fig. 3). Only seven diatom species were found in the bog pool sediments, primarily Frustulia rhomboides (Mayer) but other minor species included Amphora spp., Eunotia indica (Grunow), Fragilaria harrisonii (Grunow), Mastogloia pseudoparadoxa (Hust), Navicula rostellata (Kutz) and Pinnularia sp. In pool 4, there were more species of diatoms than in the bog pool. Thirteen species were found and the dominant species were Amphora weissflogii (A. Schmidt) and Eunotia indica. In pool 6, 10 species of diatoms were found and the dominant species were Fragilaria harrisonii (W. Smith), Navicula biformis (Grunow) and Melosira spp. Concentrations of diatoms in the bog pool, 9 and in pool 4 were much lower than those in pool 6. Springer

Distinct Optical Chemistry of Dissolved Organic Matter in Urban Pond Ecosystems Nicola A. McEnroe1, Clayton J. Williams1, Marguerite A. Xenopoulos1, Petr Porcal2, Paul C. Frost1* 1 Department of Biology, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario, Canada, 2 Biology Centre of the Academy of Science of the Czech Republic, v.v.i., Institute of Hydrobiology, České Budějovice, Czech Republic Abstract Urbanization has the potential to dramatically alter the biogeochemistry of receiving freshwater ecosystems. We examined the optical chemistry of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in forty-five urban ponds across southern Ontario, Canada to examine whether optical characteristics in these relatively new ecosystems are distinct from other freshwater systems. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations ranged from 2 to 16 mg C L⁻¹ across the ponds with an average value of 5.3 mg C L⁻¹. Excitation-emission matrix (EEM) spectroscopy and parallel factor analysis (PARAFAC) modelling showed urban pond DOM to be characterized by microbial-like and, less importantly, by terrestrial derived humic-like components. The relatively transparent, non-humic DOM in urban ponds was more similar to that found in open water, lake ecosystems than to rivers or wetlands. After irradiation equivalent to 1.7 days of natural solar radiation, DOC concentrations, on average, decreased by 38% and UV absorbance decreased by 25%. Irradiation decreased the relative abundances of terrestrial humic-like components and increased protein-like aspects of the DOM pool. These findings suggest that high internal production and/or prolonged exposure to sunlight exerts a distinct and significant influence on the chemistry of urban pond DOM, which likely reduces its chemical similarity with upstream sources. These properties of urban pond DOM may alter its biogeochemical role in these relatively novel aquatic ecosystems. Competing interests: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist. * E-mail: paulfrost@trentu.ca Introduction In the last few decades, urbanization has been associated with widespread loss of natural (wetlands and forest) and agricultural areas [1]. This landscape conversion has been accompanied by greater imperviousness of watersheds to infiltration by surface waters and altered hydrological cycles (e.g., [2,3]). To mitigate flash flooding created by rapid drainage from highly impervious surfaces, newer urban landscapes often contain relatively shallow ponds (depth of ~2 m or less). While primarily built to retain and slow the downstream movement of stormwater, these ecosystems also potentially improve water quality through the retention of suspended sediments and dissolved nutrients [4]. Urban ponds are also thought to provide important ecological function by increasing biodiversity, serving as wildlife habitat, and altering biogeochemical cycles [5,6]. The biogeochemical role (especially for elements other than phosphorus) that urban ponds play in the developed landscape has not been well-studied, despite potential management implications. One study based on 26 urban stormwater ponds reported high rates of microbial activity and biogeochemical processes suggesting that, at current pond density, they could play an important role in regional and global carbon (C) cycles [7]. Other small, shallow freshwater systems are also typically characterized by disproportionately high rates of nutrient processing compared to larger bodies of water [8]. For example, sedimentation rates and burial of organic C can be higher in small freshwater bodies than in larger aquatic ecosystems [9-11]. In addition, allochthonous derived DOM has been shown to fuel surprising quantities of microbial production in small aquatic ecosystems and to support freshwater food webs beyond that provided by primary production alone (e.g., [12-15]). While not particularly well-studied, urban land use has been reported to increase the loading of dissolved organic matter (DOM) above levels found in natural areas due to changes in soil and drainage conditions [16]. In contrast, DOM concentrations in streams have been observed to decrease post-urbanisation due to the loss of hydrological flow paths through shallow soils [17,18]. Either way, DOM characteristics from such areas may differ from that seen in waters emerging from more natural (e.g., forested and wetland) or agricultural areas [19,20]. For example, DOM derived from urban wastewater can be distinguished from the DOM in receiving river systems through point-source increases in protein-like DOM resolved by fluorescence characterization [21]. DOM arising within urban aquatic ecosystems may have different transparency, humicity, molecular weight, and/or photoreactivity arising from limited contact with organic soils and vegetation in urban watersheds. If so, exported DOM from these urban environments could be less colored, more transparent, and/or have other, distinct fluorescent properties. The source and chemical properties of urban pond DOM could affect the rate of DOM microbial decomposition and photodegradation. Autochthonous DOM tends to be more aliphatic and less aromatic in character compared to terrestrial derived DOM (e.g., [22]). These properties have been found to limit DOM photoreactivity (e.g., [23-25]). Photodegradation can result in more biologically available substrates (e.g., [26]) or could increase DOM humicity, reducing its bioavailability (e.g., [24,27-30]). However, how DOM in these urban ponds changes in response to exposure to solar radiation remains unknown. In this study, we first examined the quantity and quality of DOM in urban ponds as it compares to DOM sampled from more natural aquatic ecosystems. We then examined the photochemical reactivity of urban pond DOM. Finally, we examined how the properties of DOM relate to indices of internal production (e.g., seston chlorophyll). We expected that urban pond DOM would have a distinct optical chemistry compared to that derived from more natural areas, based on either greater contributions of anthropogenic derived organic matter or from high autochthonous production. We further expected that these unique chemical properties would affect rates of in-situ photochemical degradation. We thus provide a thorough examination of DOM and its chemistry in stormwater retention ponds. Methods Ethics Statement All field sites were accessed by public right of way and did not require explicit permission from the municipality to collect water. Because we only collected water samples, none of our field work involved threatened or endangered species. Sample sites We examined DOM properties in forty-five urban ponds in four municipalities in southern Ontario, Canada (Ottawa, Peterborough, Richmond Hill and Whitby). Selected ponds were all in residential areas and have variable catchment and drainage properties (Table 1). Additional information about these ponds and their biogeochemistry is provided in [7,31]. We compared our DOM data on urban pond water with previously published data that we compiled from studies of non-urban, aquatic environments to determine whether their DOM characteristics match that seen in natural ecosystems. Comparison data were taken from studies of different types of aquatic environments including forested and wetland-dominated streams, saline lakes, and eutrophic to hypereutrophic inland water bodies. Ambient DOM characteristics We sampled water in ponds twice (June and August) during the summer of 2009. Whole water samples were collected at the deepest part of each pond at the surface (0-10 cm) and at the water-sediment interface (~0.5-2.7 m, Table 1) using a Van Dorn sampler. These samples were placed into deionized water (DI) rinsed, acid washed polypropylene bottles and held on ice in the dark during transport back to the laboratory. Within 24 hours, we filtered samples (Whatman Type polycarbonate PCTE, 0.2 μm) and placed this water into acid washed and pre-combusted glass amber bottles, which were refrigerated at 4°C until further analysis. Concentrations of DOC (mg C L^{-1}) in each sample were determined using a TOC-TN Analyser (Model 1030D OI Analytical Aurora, Texas, USA) after combustion (750°C) and acidification with 2 N hydrochloric acid. UV-visible absorbance were measured on each sample between 200 and 800 nm (Perkin Elmer Lambda 25 Spectrophotometer) and the absorption coefficient (a_{nm}) was determined by multiplying absorbance (A_{nm}) by 2.303 and dividing by the path length in meters following [32]. Molar absorptivity at 280 and 350 nm (\epsilon_{280}, \epsilon_{350}) was calculated as absorbance (A_{nm}) at 280 and 350 nm divided by the DOC concentration (μmol C L^{-1}; [33]). Absorbance at 440 nm (A_{440}) was used as an additional indicator of DOC color [34]. DOM optical characteristics To determine DOM fluorescence characteristics of urban pond water, we selected a subset of ponds from August sampling (n=25, Table 1) for excitation emission matrix (EEM) measurements. EEM measurements on surface water samples from these ponds were made using fluorescence spectroscopy (Varian Eclipse Fluorometer, 5 nm bandwidth, integration time 0.25 s), over a range of emission (270-600 nm, 2 nm intervals) and excitation (230-500 nm, 5 nm intervals) wavelengths. The EEMs were corrected for inner filter effects [22,35], and for second-order Raman and Rayleigh scatter effects and instrument bias using manufacturer recommended instrument settings. Milli-Q water blank EEM fluorescence was subtracted from that of sample EEMs and EEMs were converted to Raman Units (RU) using the area under the Milli-Q Raman scatter peak at excitation 350 nm. To investigate DOM fluorescence parameters, EEM data were used to calculate the humification index (HIX), fluorescence index (FI) and β:α ratio. The HIX was calculated as the ratio of peak area under each curve at emission 434-480 nm and 300-346 nm after excitation at 255 nm [36]. The FI was calculated, using an excitation wavelength of 370 nm, as the ratio of emission intensities at 470 and 520 nm after [22], and β:α ratio was calculated, using an excitation wavelength of 310 nm, from emission intensity at 380 nm (β region), divided by the emission intensity maximum observed between 420 and 435 nm (α region; [20,37]). A spectral slope ratio (Sr; [38]) was determined as the ratio of the log-transformed slope between 275 to 295 and 350 to 400 nm, Table 1. Selected characteristics of urban ponds in this study.

Landuse=R(residential), I(industrial), M(mixed), H(highway); BSS= Bottom sampling depth; A0=Pond surface area; %I=impervious surface. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0080334.t001 A seven component PARAFAC (Parallel Factor Analysis) model was used to examine factors of each EEM (Matlab 2012b, Mathworks; Figure 1). EEMs collected during the photo-irradiation experiment were fit to the PARAFAC model and residuals were visually examined to verify model fit. The full model validation and description is presented in detail in [7]. Of the seven PARAFAC components, C1 resembles humic-like material and occurs in most ecosystems [39,40]. C2 and C3 appear similar to humic-like DOM of terrestrial origin [41]. C4 resembles the fluorescence signatures of soil, fulvic acid-like substances [42]. C5 and C6 are similar to microbial derived humic-like substances [7,19,39]. C7 resembles protein-like materials [21,42] as well as photodegradable plant tannin-protein complexes [43]. The PARAFAC components are expressed as relative abundance (% of Fmax). DOM photo-irradiation The same samples (n=25) collected from the pond surface were included in photo-irradiation experiments. For these experiments, aliquots (25 ml) of filtered pond water were transferred into DI-water rinsed, sterile UV-transparent polyethylene bags and the samples were irradiated using a XE Arc lamp (500 W m2 for 12 hours; Suntest XLS+ Solar Simulator, 2220W lamp, internal water bath temperature of 25°C, Atlas, Germany) approximating the solar spectral quality at sea level. Control samples treated as irradiated samples (membrane filtration and stored in polyethylene bags) were wrapped in aluminium foil and exposed to the same temperature as irradiated samples inside the solar simulator. The radiation intensity of 500 W m2 is equivalent to a radiant energy dosage of 21.6 MJ m2, or to 1.7 days of natural solar radiation in June at our study location, based on estimates of the monthly averaged insolation on a horizontal surface (NASA Surface Meteorology and Solar Energy data; http://eosweb.larc.nasa.gov). The transformation of cumulative irradiation energy to the number of corresponding days of natural irradiation was done by dividing the cumulative energy by averaged insolation energy at the sampling location. Changes in DOC concentrations during photo-irradiation are expressed against cumulative irradiation energy, which is the product of intensity of irradiation and time. The decrease in DOC with cumulative irradiation energy followed exponential decrease as observed in other studies (e.g. [44,45]). Thus the pseudo first order kinetics rate constant was used as a measure of DOC photodegradation in individual samples, following: \[ DOC = (DOC_0 - DOC_R) \equiv \exp(-k_{DOC}E) + DOC_R \] Where DOC0 is the initial DOC concentration, DOCR is the concentration of DOC that remained after the experiment, \( k_{DOC} \) is the photochemical degradation rate constant (m2 MJ-1) and E is the cumulative energy of irradiation (MJ m-2; see 45). Indices of production in urban ponds We examined how urban pond DOM properties related to indices of production: seston chlorophyll, dissolved oxygen (DO) and total phosphorus (TP) concentrations. Seston chlorophyll concentrations on filtered samples (Whatman Type GF/F, 25 mm) were determined after ethanol cold extraction (24 h) with fluorometry (440 nm excitation, 660 nm emission Figure 1. Countor plots of seven component PARAFAC model. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0080334.g001 wavelengths). Profiles of water column DO were obtained from the deepest part of each pond from the surface and every 10-20 cm depth to the water sediment interface (YSI Model 54 Oxygen Meter, Yellow Springs Instrument Co., Yellow Springs, Ohio, USA). TP concentrations were determined on unfiltered water samples stored at 4°C in acid washed polypropylene and pre-combusted (500°C) amber glass bottles, using potassium persulfate digestion (autoclave at 121°C) followed by ascorbic acid-sodium molybdate blue colorimetric analyses (Spectrophotometer, Biochrome Ultrospec Pro 500, 885 nm wavelength). Statistical analyses Prior to statistical analysis, most data were transformed (log(y) or square root (y)) to meet the assumptions of normality and homoscedasticity. Pearson’s Correlation analyses were used to determine significant relationships (α = 0.05) between DOM UV absorbance and fluorescence indices. One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) or Student’s t-test was used to determine statistically significant differences between means, followed by the Tukey-Kramer HSD post hoc test where differences were found (α = 0.05). Permutational Multivariate (M)ANOVA with post hoc comparison was used to determine the overall impact of photo-irradiance on fluorescent DOM. MANOVA results were visualized using Principle Component Analysis. Statistical analyses were carried out using JMP v.9 (SAS Institute, 2009), PASW Statistics 18 (SPSS Inc., 2009), and R with the VEGAN library. Results Ambient DOM characteristics In the entire dataset for 45 urban ponds, including both sampling dates and depths, DOC concentrations ranged between 2.0 to 16.2 mg L⁻¹ (mean ± SD; 5.3 ± 1.9 mg L⁻¹). On average, DOC concentrations were lower in June (p = 0.04, 4.9 mg C L⁻¹) compared to August (5.7 mg C L⁻¹). While molar absorptivity (ε₂₈₀) was significantly higher in June (p < 0.001), absorbance at 280 (a₂₈₀; Table 2) and 440 nm (a₄₄₀; Table 1) were not different between sampling dates and showed a wide range among sampled ponds. From the subset of urban ponds selected for more detailed optical characterization (n=25), DOC concentrations ranged from 3.2 to 8.2 mg L⁻¹ (mean ± SD; 5.03 ± 1.04 mg L⁻¹) and fluorescence indices were found to vary considerably (Figure 2; Table 2). DOC concentrations were positively correlated with FI and UV-visible absorbance and were negatively correlated with molar absorptivity (ε₂₈₀; Table 3). While PARAFAC component C6 (anthropogenic/microbial humic-like) was generally the most abundant (23 - 52%) and C4 (soil fulvic acid-like) was the least abundant (2 - 5%), the relative abundance of the individual components varied among ponds (Figure 3). In 20% of samples, photo-irradiation had no effect on DOC concentrations with net irradiation rate constants ranging from 0 to 0.02 m$^2$ MJ$^{-1}$. Despite this, photo-irradiation decreased DOC concentrations, on average, by 38%. We also observed decreases in absorbance ($A_{nm}$) and fluorescence indices in samples exposed to light relative to the dark controls ($p < 0.05$; Figure 2). While average absorbance ($A_{nm}$) was reduced by 25% in the UVA and UVB regions, average molar absorptivity ($\varepsilon_{280}$) increased by 30% in light exposed samples relative to the dark controls. Photo-irradiation altered characteristics of DOM quality indexed by PARAFAC, but these effects depended on the component examined (Figure 3). Among all ponds, the intensity C1 to C6 ($F_{max}$; RU) decreased after light exposure. The intensity of C7 (RU), however, responded non-uniformly to light exposure among ponds. C7 (RU) increased, decreased, or was similar to initial $F_{max}$ depending on the pond water examined. The relative abundance (%) of C4 and C6 were not significantly different from initial levels after dark and light incubations ($p = 0.753$ and $p = 0.095$, respectively). C1 (%) and C2 (%) were significantly lower after light exposure relative to the dark incubation ($p = 0.039$ and $p = 0.027$, respectively). Photo-irradiation also significantly decreased C5 (%; $p < 0.001$) and increased C3 (%; $p < 0.001$) and C7 (%; $p < 0.001$) from dark incubated and initial treatments. The relative abundance of C1 consistently correlated positively with HIX and negatively with $\beta:\alpha$ across initial, light, and dark treatments (Figure 4). Correlations between C7, HIX, and $\beta:\alpha$, however, were influenced by photo-irradiation (Figure 4). Light treated samples had higher levels of C7 and lower levels of HIX than initial and dark samples and had a similar correlation slope overall. C7 positively related to $\beta:\alpha$ for initial samples, but this relationship was not preserved after photo-irradiation. Overall, photo-irradiation significantly impacted the fluorescent DOM pool (MANOVA, $p = 0.001$), which appeared to be strongly influenced by changes in C7 (Figure 5). Index of urban pond production We found that DOC concentrations (negatively) and $\varepsilon_{280}$ (positively) were correlated with chlorophyll whereas no other optical property of the DOM was related to this index of productivity (Figure 6). $S_r$ (negatively), HIX (positively), and $\varepsilon_{280}$ (positively) significantly correlated with total phosphorus. Only $S_r$ and $\beta:\alpha$ related to dissolved oxygen concentrations in the surface waters of urban ponds (Figure 6). Of the seven PARAFAC components, we found that seston chlorophyll and total phosphorus was positively correlated with C4 and C5 and negatively correlated with C3 and C7 (Figure 6). Discussion We examined the quantity and chemistry of DOM in ponds embedded within highly urbanized environments and report the change in its optical chemistry after irradiation. We expected that DOM in urban ponds would have a distinct optical chemistry compared to that derived from more natural areas. This predicted difference was based on our expectations of greater contributions of either anthropogenic-derived organic matter (of a distinct composition) or from high internal production of DOM. We found that urban pond DOM was relatively transparent (low \( \varepsilon_{280} \)) and uncolored (low \( a_{440} \)), had lower HIX and higher \( \beta:\alpha \) ratios compared to reported values for numerous temperate lakes and streams, and some other anthropogenic impacted waters. DOM in urban ponds nonetheless contained a unique mixture of microbial and terrestrial derived C, reflected in the HIX index [36], FI and β:α ratio values [39,46] (Table 1). The DOM pool was dominated by a likely algal-derived humic-like component (C6) with relatively low percentages of terrestrial-like components (Figure 3). C6 was much more abundant in urban ponds than in natural freshwaters in the same geographical region (e.g., southern Ontario [19];; C. Williams, unpublished data). It could be argued that urban ponds should not be dominated by autochthonous C, given their role in overland flood control and engineered connectivity with the watershed. The lack of terrestrial DOM influence on pond DOM may simply reflect the reduced presence of natural components (e.g. vegetation, soils, etc.) of the upstream catchment. Urban streams, however, can contain high amounts of terrestrial DOM [19,40] and we expected a stronger signal of this DOM within urban ponds. These ecosystems could either Figure 4. Future studies should focus on determining the relative importance of terrestrial DOM sources and internal processing rates on urban pond DOM chemistry, in part, by examining the timing and importance of external water inputs. The urban ponds in our study are downstream of stormwater drainage systems designed to channel runoff very quickly, which may further limit contact with soils and vegetation within the upstream catchment. Our results contrast with other freshwater ecosystems where allochthonous C is usually assumed to be the major fraction of DOM (e.g., [47]) due to high hydrologic connectivity between rivers and lakes and their upstream undeveloped watersheds. Figure 5. Principle components plot with vector loadings for the fluorescent DOM pool. MANOVA with post hoc test indicated that the light exposed fluorescent DOM pool (closed circles) was significantly different than initial (open circles) and dark (triangles) pools, which did not differ. Note, vector loadings for β:α and FI were near the origin in the first two PCA dimensions and are not displayed in this figure. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0080334.g005 The distinct character of urban pond DOM from that found in natural streams and lakes in the same region and other aquatic ecosystems largely resulted from the greater prominence of relatively transparent, internally-produced DOM. This has also been reported in other anthropogenically impacted water bodies that are relatively nutrient rich (e.g., [48] and references therein) as well as in mixotrophic to eutrophic, saline lakes (e.g., [49]). An algal-derived humic-like component (C6) was the most abundant in urban ponds and represented about 52% of the DOM fluorescence pools. C6 was higher in ponds with lower HIX scores, indicating that DOM with this chemical feature is produced internally and dilutes the allochthonous DOM pools. This component type has been documented in other human impacted areas and in highly productive ecosystems (e.g., [50]), which is further indication that there is significant internal production of DOC in urban ponds [7,41]. Figure 6. Correlation coefficients between DOC concentration (mg C L^{-1}), optical properties, and PARAFAC components and seston chlorophyll (dark bars), TP (light bars) and DO (open bars). Significant correlations (\( p<0.05 \)) are noted with *. doi: 10.1371/journal.pone.0080334.g006 Urban pond DOM thus appears to have a distinct chemical signature that originates from primary production, which is fueled by high nutrient loading in these heavily urbanized catchments. Due to its relative transparency and low aromaticity, the major DOM fraction in urban ponds should be particularly resistant to photochemical transformation. In fact, the main component of the DOM pool (C6) was not impacted significantly by light exposure. This result is similar to that reported for pelagic algal-derived DOM and DOM in some eutrophic ecosystems, which have relatively low rates of photomineralization [26]. Similarly, we also found no DOC loss with light exposure in about one fifth of our pond samples. This lack of significant total DOM photodegradation might simply reflect the chemical properties of internally produced DOM in these urban ponds. Especially transparent autochthonous material should not be photo-oxidative [25]. On the other hand, DOM in urban ponds may have already experienced prolonged UVR exposure prior to sampling, especially if there had been no recent hydrological inputs from the watershed. We would expect that rates of photochemical degradation should be higher in water samples obtained directly from in-flowing stormwater. Future comparative studies of DOM properties and photodegradation of fresh stormwater and *in situ* urban pond water would be useful to differentiate between these controls. The less abundant terrestrial derived components of the urban pond DOM pool were the most sensitive to photochemical degradation. After photo-irradiation, DOM fluorescence shifted from humic-like to protein-like, with decreases in the most terrestrial humic-like components (C1, C2, and C5) and significant increases a protein-like component (C7; Figure 3). One terrestrial, humic-like component (C3) increased after photo-irradiation, which suggests that this component is photo-stable or photo-produced [41]. This indicates that C3 might be a product of photodegradation of the other terrestrial components. Given these changes in photo-exposed DOM samples, natural measurements of these rates of gain and losses in urban ponds over time would be a logical next step to better understand the controls of the DOM pool in these urban freshwater ecosystems. Nevertheless, DOM chemistry in urban ponds appears to be controlled by a combination of processes (i.e., DOM import, release from primary producers, and photoirradiation), which would all act in concert to shape the overall properties of this important energy source to microbial communities. We found DOC concentration decreased in many pond samples under irradiation, but losses were also observed in some samples held in the dark. This dark-sample decrease in DOC concentration likely resulted from microbial activity [51]. While samples were filtered prior to the photo-exposure experiment, remnant microbial communities could nonetheless have consumed labile components of the DOM. The decrease in DOC concentration in dark samples was not reflected by corresponding changes in absorbance and is consistent with losses of low molecular-weight labile substrates with low absorbance. These same decreases in labile substrates with low absorbance were observed in irradiated samples, which is indicated by the increase in \( \varepsilon_{280} \) that would have been produced by a smaller decrease in absorbance compared to DOC concentration. A recent review by [52] showed variability in bacterial responses during irradiation ranging from stimulation to inhibition. However, irradiating with a full range of artificial UVA and UVB inhibited microbial growth, perhaps due to photoproduction of singlet oxygen and other reactive oxygen species [53-55]. Singlet oxygen is the primary agent of photo-oxidative stress in microorganisms [56] and high concentrations may delay consumption of the readily decomposable portions of the DOM until dark conditions prevail. Thus the microbial degradation in irradiated samples likely took place after irradiation rather than simultaneously with irradiation. The dark-sample losses nonetheless suggest that some changes observed in the photo-exposed samples resulted from the experimental conditions (i.e., non-sterility of bags) and not light per se. However, compared to the rates observed in the light exposed samples, this effect was minimal and does not significantly affect rate measurements or the observed photo-induced changes in DOM chemistry. Chlorophyll concentrations are one surrogate index of algal biomass and should be correlated with the internal production of autochthonous DOC in freshwater ecosystems (e.g., [57]). Consequently, we expected that algal biomass in the urban ponds to be positively related to concentrations of the highly transparent DOM. Our results are not entirely consistent with this expectation as HIX and \( \varepsilon_{280} \) (both indicators of terrestrial DOM) were positively correlated with TP and chlorophyll. This result suggests that the connections between TP, productivity, and DOM chemistry are likely more complex than the simple scenario previously described. For example, greater primary production coincides with higher TP concentration in urban ponds but this may have contrasting effects on the DOM and its chemistry. While internal productivity may contribute transparent DOM and dilute terrestrial sources, it may also fuel (along with the higher nutrient concentrations) greater microbial activity that could reduce DOM concentrations. The negative relationships between chlorophyll and TP with C7 are consistent with these indirect connections. Future work should thus better examine the how DOM chemistry relates to primary producers and their external nutrient controls in urban environments. We found a prominent signature of internally derived DOM in urban ponds of this study. This unique chemical signature likely reflects a dominance of internally produced C, the lack of external humic sources, and considerable microbial and photo-processing. While this unique chemical signature differentiates urban pond DOM from other aquatic ecosystems, how it affects the pond physical (light penetration), chemical (metal binding), or biological (microbial production) processes remains largely to be seen. Given their growing abundance and important role in urban water cycles, these ponds would appear to be potential hotspots for C processing in the urban landscape and warrant further examination of their carbon cycling. EEMs collected during the photo-irradiation experiment were fit to the PARAFAC model and residuals were visually examined to verify model fit. The full model validation and description is presented in detail in [7]. Of the seven PARAFAC components, C1 resembles humic-like material and occurs in most ecosystems [39,40]. C2 and C3 appear similar to humic-like DOM of terrestrial origin [41]. C4 resembles the fluorescence signatures of soil, fulvic acid-like substances [42]. C5 and C6 are similar to microbial derived humic-like substances [7,19,39]. C7 resembles protein-like materials [21,42] as well as photodegradable plant tannin-protein complexes [43]. The PARAFAC components are expressed as relative abundance (% of Fmax). DOM photo-irradiation The same samples (n=25) collected from the pond surface were included in photo-irradiation experiments. For these experiments, aliquots (25 ml) of filtered pond water were transferred into DI-water rinsed, sterile UV-transparent polyethylene bags and the samples were irradiated using a XE Arc lamp (500 W m2 for 12 hours; Suntest XLS+ Solar Simulator, 2220W lamp, internal water bath temperature of 25°C, Atlas, Germany) approximating the solar spectral quality at sea level. Control samples treated as irradiated samples (membrane filtration and stored in polyethylene bags) were wrapped in aluminium foil and exposed to the same temperature as irradiated samples inside the solar simulator. The radiation intensity of 500 W m2 is equivalent to a radiant energy dosage of 21.6 MJ m2, or to 1.7 days of natural solar radiation in June at our study location, based on estimates of the monthly averaged insolation on a horizontal surface (NASA Surface Meteorology and Solar Energy data; http://eosweb.larc.nasa.gov). The transformation of cumulative irradiation energy to the number of corresponding days of natural irradiation was done by dividing the cumulative energy by averaged insolation energy at the sampling location. Changes in DOC concentrations during photo-irradiation are expressed against cumulative irradiation energy, which is the product of intensity of irradiation and time. The decrease in DOC with cumulative irradiation energy followed exponential decrease as observed in other studies (e.g. [44,45]). Thus the pseudo first order kinetics rate constant was used as a measure of DOC photodegradation in individual samples, following: \[ DOC = (DOC_0 - DOC_R) \equiv \exp(-k_{DOC}E) + DOC_R \] Where DOC0 is the initial DOC concentration, DOCR is the concentration of DOC that remained after the experiment, \( k_{DOC} \) is the photochemical degradation rate constant (m2 MJ-1) and E is the cumulative energy of irradiation (MJ m-2; see 45). Diversity of macroinvertebrates positively correlates with diversity of macrophytes in karst ponds Igor Zelnik*, Neža Gregorič, Ana Tratnik University of Ljubljana, Biotechnical Faculty, Department of Biology, Jamnikarjeva 101, SI-1000 Ljubljana, Slovenia ARTICLE INFO Keywords: Emergent macrophytes Karst ponds Montane pastures South-eastern calcareous Alps Slovenia ABSTRACT Relations between diversity of macrophytes and macroinvertebrates in 16 karst ponds on the outskirts of SE Alps (Slovenia) were investigated. Inventory of macrophytes was performed and their cover values were estimated. Macroinvertebrates were sampled with hand net. Correlations between environmental factors and parameters of taxonomic richness and diversity of the communities were calculated. Influences of environmental parameters on the structure of communities were analyzed. Results confirmed significant positive correlations between diversity of macrophytes and macroinvertebrates. The most abundant and most species-rich group of plants were emergent macrophytes. Richness and diversity of macrophytes were more important than their coverage for diversity of macroinvertebrates. A negative direct influence of the cattle to macrophytes as well as to macroinvertebrates was calculated. We can conclude that diversity of macrophytes had a positive influence on diversity of macroinvertebrate community. High diversity of emergent macrophytes supports high diversity of macroinvertebrate communities – directly as higher number of hiding places, oviposition sites or food sources and indirectly with more efficient uptake of excessive nutrients. Despite the negative direct influence of the cattle to macrophytes that we calculated, trampling positively influences macrophytes and indirectly also macroinvertebrates in karst ponds, since it enables the existence of these specific waterbodies in the long run. 1. Introduction Ponds are waterbodies shallow enough that light can reach the bottom in the entire ecosystem and enable photosynthesis and high number of ecological niches (Wetzel, 2001). Ponds also fall in the scope of wetlands according to definition by Ramsar convention and amended definition by Gopal (2016), respectively. Unlike the lakes, surface of a pond is lower than 2 hectares (De Meester et al., 2005; Hassall et al., 2011). Despite their small size, ponds have a great biodiversity which is relatively higher than in lakes and watercourses (Williams et al., 2004; Biggs et al., 2005; Davies et al., 2008). Ponds have different ecological functioning than lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2005) also because of their higher perimeter:area ratio which enhances biogeochemical functions (Marton et al., 2015; Cohen et al., 2016), so the rate of nutrient cycling is higher than in lakes (Wetzel, 2001). Ponds in alpine regions have been less studied than lakes (Hamerlik et al., 2014), but their relatively higher diversity emphasizes their relevance for regional diversity in mountain areas (Hamerlik et al., 2014). Since the conservation of freshwaters has fallen behind the conservation of terrestrial ecosystems (Stendera et al., 2012), alpine ponds offer an opportunity to partly fill that gap. 1.1. Karst ponds Karst ponds are small artificial lentic waterbodies made to collect and store rainwater in karstic landscapes where there are no natural surface waterbodies. Their primary role of being a water supply has been accompanied, in last decades, by their significant contribution to biodiversity (Zelnik et al., 2012). Existence, diversity and quality of karst ponds depend on human activities. Activity which is most tightly connected with them is grazing by cattle and in some places horses. Mountain pasture depends on sufficient number of karst ponds containing water of considerable quality which is often difficult to provide. Protection of karst ponds from pollution is possible only with suitable management of ponds and their catchments, respectively. Harrison et al. (2017) report that grazing can alter wetland productivity and diversity by removing or trampling vegetation, compacting soil, increasing erosion, and adding nutrients. 1.2. Communities of macrophytes and macroinvertebrates in ponds Few studies have simultaneously evaluated plant and animal communities in ponds (e.g., Oertli et al., 2002; Nicolet et al., 2004; Landi et al., 2012). Bagella et al. (2010) argue that simultaneous survey of several communities would enable a better understanding of ecosystem functionality. Different aquatic communities respond differently to environmental factors, so biodiversity patterns and factors which determine them cannot be generalized to other communities (Gascón et al., 2009). Macrophytes are an important structural element of aquatic ecosystems and sustain biodiversity (Hassall et al., 2011; Ilg and Oertli, 2014), since they increase number of mesohabitats for invertebrates (Heino, 2000; Robin et al., 2014). Moreover, they are essential for ecosystem functioning and for reaching a good ecological status of aquatic ecosystems. Abundance and diversity of macrophytes depend on water quality, depth and substrate characteristics (Baattrup-Pedersen and Riis, 1999), but they also affect water quality, so they have direct and indirect impacts on diversity of macroinvertebrates. Their preservation requires sufficient knowledge on how plant communities are controlled by environmental factors (Bornette and Puijalon, 2011), but there are still important gaps in such knowledge (Chappuis et al., 2011). Significant positive correlations between diversity of macrophyte and invertebrate communities in ponds has been reported in studies conducted in different European regions like Alpine (Oertli et al., 2002, 2008; Ilg and Oertli 2014), Mediterranean (Della Bella et al., 2008; Bagella et al., 2010) and Atlantic (Nicolet et al., 2004; Hassall et al., 2011). Macrophytes increase heterogeneity of the habitat, providing shelters, living space, oviposition sites and food for macroinvertebrates (Jeppesen et al., 1997; Wetzel, 2001). Environmental factors that drive pond biodiversity are specific to region (Alvarez Cobelas et al., 2005; De Marco et al., 2014) as well as to elevation range (Hindem et al., 2005; Fernández-Alaez, 2017). Based on these findings mountain ponds should be treated differently than lowland ponds and different management plans should be implemented. We hypothesized that i) composition of macrophyte and macroinvertebrate communities will be influenced by different sets of environmental variables characteristic to the region and elevation; ii) that species richness and diversity of macrophytes positively correlates with richness and diversity of macroinvertebrates; iii) while intensity of grazing negatively influences the diversity of both studied communities. 2. Material and methods 2.1. Study area Macrophyte and macroinvertebrate communities as well as selected environmental variables in 16 karst ponds located mostly on karst plateaus were analyzed. Studied ponds were selected using satellite images of pasture landscapes in different parts of SE calcareous Alps that occur in NW and N Slovenia to avoid biased selection in the field. Selected ponds can be found in montane and subalpine belt at altitudes between 1000 and 1800 m a.s.l. in Alpine region of Slovenia, where mountain pastures are widespread and grazed by cattle during the summer. Altitude and coordinates (Gauss-Krüger system) of each pond was obtained with GPS device (Table 1). Data on average annual precipitation was found in Cegnar (2003). Karst ponds were sampled during the summer in the year 2014 from July 1 to September 5, beginning at lower altitudes and ending at the highest sites. The climate is alpine with enough rain during the summer months to maintain permanent ponds despite being used by cattle. 2.2. Macrophyte survey Macrophytes were recorded and their cover values in percentage scale were estimated. Macrophyte were classified in different groups according to Ellenberg’s indicator value (EIV) for humidity of the site (Ellenberg et al., 2001), like submerged or emergent macrophytes or flood-meadow taxa (Table 2). 2.3. Macroinvertebrate survey MI were sampled according to modified PLOCH method described in Oertli et al. (2005), which suggests sampling in two habitats – in land-water interface, which represents the edge of the pond, and the bottom of the pond, which is the central part of the pond. Firstly the assessment of substrata was performed and cover values (in %) of specific substrate categories were estimated. Afterwards from 6 to 8 sampling plots were selected according to the size of the pond to cover both habitats as well as most representative mesohabitats within them. Quantitative sampling of various substrata (mesohabitats) was performed with hand-net 25 × 25 cm, (pores 0.5 × 0.5 mm) from the plot of 25 × 50 cm for 30 s. Samples were fixed and stored for further analyses in laboratory. Determination to the level of family was done with the help of determination keys in Tachet et al. (2010). Abundance of each taxon was expressed as the share of individuals counted in the sample. 2.4. Environmental factors At each sampling pH, water temperature, electric conductivity, oxygen concentration and saturation were measured with multimeter (EUTECH, PCD 650). Turbidity of the water was measured as Secchi depth. Water samples were analyzed in laboratory for concentrations of: TP, PO4^{3-}, NO3-N, NH4-N, TN, as well as TSS and TDS. The cuvette tests HACH Lange were performed for the content of ammonium (LCK 304), nitrate (LCK 339) and phosphate (LCK 349). We measured the concentrations with the spectrophotometer HACH Lange LT 200. Water depth was also measured, as well as the surface parameters (length and width or diameter) which were used for calculation of approximate surface and volume. Types and proportions of inorganic and organic substrate (%) were surveyed according to classification by AQEM (2002). Biotic parameters were also estimated – like cover of the pond surface (%) with tree canopies, abundance (%) of woody species (willows), abundance (%) of filamentous algae. We estimated the share of trampled banks expressed as the percentage of the pond perimeter as well as the intensity of trampling on a six-degree scale: 0 = no signs of trampling; 1 = single hoof-prints, without significant influence on vegetation; 2 = groups of hoof-prints, no major influence on vegetation; 3 = trampled areas with strips of bare ground within remaining strips of vegetation; 4 = intensively trampled areas with only some bunches of remaining vegetation; 5 = completely trampled area, bare ground. Characteristics of the catchment area around each pond were surveyed as the number of habitat types within 10 m as well as 50 m from the water edge. Moreover, land-use intensity within 50 m from the pond was estimated on a five-degree scale: 5 = undisturbed forest (negligible human influence); 4 = mixture of forest and grassland; 3 = extensively grazed pastures, grassland/forest; 2 = extensively grazed pastures; 1 = intensively grazed pastures. 2.5. Diversity indices Richness of macrophytes was expressed as the number of species of: all vascular plants (VP), aquatic macrophytes (AM), emergent macrophytes (EM), submerged macrophytes (SM) and flood-meadow species (Table 2). Richness of macroinvertebrate community was expressed as number of families determined in the samples and as the number of higher taxa (e.g., order, subclass). Heterogeneity or diversity of macroinvertebrates was calculated as Shannon-Wiener (S-W) diversity index and Margalef (Mrg) diversity index on the base of shares of families as well as higher taxa. For both communities abundances were also determined. In case of macrophytes cover values were used, while in case of macroinvertebrate number of individuals of each taxon in the sample were counted. 2.6. Statistic analyses Relations between diversity indices and structural elements of both communities were calculated using Spearman correlations on ranks, as well as between diversity indices and environmental factors to find direct relations between diversity and specific elements of the communities with environmental factors. The influence of specific environmental factors on the taxonomic composition of studied communities were checked by direct gradient analysis. Firstly, we conducted a detrended correspondence analysis (DCA), which showed linear distribution in case of macroinvertebrates and slow turnover of taxonomic data along potential gradients (gradient length = 1.81 S.D., eigenvalue of 1st axis = 0.214), so we used redundancy analysis (RDA). In case of macrophytes we got different result (gradient length = 3.11 S.D., eigenvalue of 1st axis = 0.559), so we used canonical correspondence analysis (CCA). Analyses were performed with the software package CANOCO 4.5 (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). Both sets of data were log transformed. With RDA and CCA, respectively, we checked the relation between species composition and selected factors, and the share of the variability of the mentioned community they explain. This was conducted with the series of RDAs and CCAs, respectively. The impact of environmental factors on species composition was examined by forward selection of variables, where 499 permutations were applied. We took into account only those who had statistically significant effect (p < 0.05). Ordination diagrams were created on the basis of the results of RDA and CCA, respectively. 3. Results Although the bedrock is more or less the same in all locations, considerable differences of physical and chemical conditions were measured (Table 3). Considering the composition of inorganic substrate, the differences were negligible (Table 4) since clay and silt dominated in all but two ponds. In pond MEN2 there was a plastic foil used instead of the impervious clayish layer, while in pond KR3 sand and gravel formed the bottom. 3.1. Different response of communities to environmental factors The most influential factors determining composition of the macrophyte community were: concentrations of TN (14.3% of TVE) and TP (9.4% of TVE) as well as coverage of the bottom with stony substrate (7.8% of TVE). These three factors significantly influenced the floristic composition of macrophyte community (Fig. 1) and together explained 31.5% of its variability. Ponds on the diagram (Fig. 1) are distributed according to relations between composition of macrophyte species and their distributions along significant gradients. Environmental factors that significantly influenced the composition of macroinvertebrate community were: Land-use in the catchment area (18% of TVE) and minimal measured O₂ saturation of the water (16% of TVE). These two factors together explained 34% of its variability. Ponds on the diagram (Fig. 2) are distributed according to relations between composition of macroinvertebrate families and their distributions along two significant gradients. 3.2. Correlations Correlations between coverage, species richness and diversity of different groups of macrophytes and macroinvertebrates are presented in Table 5. Correlations between richness and diversity of macroinvertebrates and environmental parameters were also calculated to find out direct relations between macroinvertebrates and abiotic factors. There was also negative correlation between diversity of macroinvertebrates and parameters of trophic status (Secchi depth, TP, nitrates). Considering the relations between abundance expressed as total coverage (TC), species richness and diversity of macrophytes and environmental factors (Table 7) the texture of the substrate turned out to be among the most important factors. The share of stony substrate had negatively correlated with diversity, richness and total coverage of AM. Trophic status, expressed as amount of TDS and concentration of NH4-N had negative influence to the species richness and diversity (S-W and Mrg index) of macrophytes. Trampling by cattle negatively correlated with diversity of AM. communities enable better understanding of ecosystem functionality in ponds. Composition of macrophyte communities were significantly influenced by concentrations of TN (14.3% of TVE) and TP (9.4% of TVE) as well as coverage of stony substrate (7.8% of TVE), which together explained 31.5% of the total variability of the vegetation. In first place, composition was driven by nutrient contents. Concentrations of nutrients are reported to have significant influence on macrophytes also by Lumbreiras et al. (2012) and Rosset et al. (2014). Fernández-Aláez et al. (2017) report conductivity and TP (together 59% of TVE) as the most important for macrophyte community composition, whereas nitrogen, which was the most important factor in our case, as not important. The share of stony substrate turned out to be the third most important factor for the variability of macrophyte community. Lacoul and Freedman (2006) also report significant influence of substrate characteristics on the structure of macrophyte community. Composition of macroinvertebrate communities was significantly influenced by land-use in the catchment area (18% of TVE) and minimal O2 saturation of water (16% of TVE), together explaining 34% of variability of the communities. Bird and Day (2016) report that composition of invertebrate community reflects land-use changes. But, these changes caused a rise in pH (Bird and Day 2016), which actually caused the change of macroinvertebrate community. In our case, land-use was most important factor that shaped the composition of macroinvertebrate community, while pH was not important. 4. Discussion 4.1. Different response of macrophyte and macroinvertebrate communities Results revealed totally different sets of environmental factors that influenced studied communities. Factors that significantly influenced the composition of macrophyte communities were concentration of TN, TP and coverage of stony substrate, while composition of macroinvertebrate communities were influenced by land-use in the catchment area and minimal O2 saturation. Similarly, Oertli et al. (2002) and Bagella et al. (2010) report that different taxonomic groups occurring in ponds showed different responses to environmental factors. We agree with Bagella et al. Positive correlations between macrophyte and invertebrate diversity in ponds has been reported from different European regions like: Alpine (Oertli et al., 2002), Mediterranean (Bazzanti et al., 2003; Bagella et al., 2010), and Atlantic (Nicolet et al., 2004). Such importance could be explained also with the conclusions (Burdett and Watts 2009) that vegetation provides trophic resources for invertebrates. Our results revealed that diversity of macrophytes was far more important for diversity of macroinvertebrates than abundance or coverage of macrophytes, although there are positive correlations reported as well (Biggs et al., 2005). The only significant positive correlations regarding this aspect were between cover of EM and mosses and diversity of macroinvertebrate families (Table 5). Moreover, we found that the richness of EM was significantly correlated with richness and diversity of macroinvertebrate community (Table 5). Fernández-Zamudio et al. (2016) also report that the edges of ponds contained a great number of EM which create a complex structure hosting a great number of macroinvertebrates. We found that abundance of Odonata highly correlated with abundance and species richness of EM and AM, respectively. Schindler et al. (2003) report that macrophyte richness influence the composition of dragonfly assemblages in ponds. Diversity of AM is important for larvae of Odonata as a refuge against predators and specific oviposition sites (De Marco et al., 2014). 4.3. Correlations between diversity of macrophyte community and environmental factors Considering the relations between diversity of macrophytes and environmental factors, the share of stony substrate significantly negatively correlated with number of VP, AM and EM, while the share of gravel and sand negatively correlated with diversity of VP and AM (Table 7). The influence of substrate characteristics on aquatic macrophyte richness has been previously reported by Lacoul and Freedman, (2006). The amount of TDS and concentration of NH4-N which mirrored trophic conditions had negative influence to the number of VP, S-W and Mrg index, as well as number of AM. This findings are in accordance with conclusion by Stendera et al. (2012) who argue that eutrophication is among the most important stressors for freshwater biodiversity. Lumbraeras et al. (2016) report that ponds in good status have a higher number of macrophyte species than less preserved. Land-use in the catchment and its changes influence the diversity of macrophyte community (Hill and Keddy 1992; Capers et al., 2010). Species richness and diversity of macrophytes did not negatively correlate with land-use in the catchment, but with the intensity and extent of trampling of the banks, which causes physical disturbance to emergent vegetation and contribute to concentration of nutrients and turbidity, which influence the structure of macrophyte communities (Mitsch and Gosselink 2000). Ponds where such disturbances are very frequent contain vegetation with lower coverage, lower number of communities as well as species (Declerck et al., 2006). On the other hand, light to moderate intensity of grazing and disturbances by cattle can be used to maintain open water in the ponds and to hinder succession with EM, which helps to maintain diverse communities (Marty, 2005). This is also in accordance with Stendera et al. (2012), who report that heterogeneity and disturbance are major drivers of freshwater biodiversity. Despite the common pattern of decreasing species richness with altitude, which is reported by many researchers (e.g. Hrivanák et al., 2013; Chappuis et al., 2011; Kochjarová et al., 2017), our results did not confirm this theory as it was not important for composition nor for diversity. 4.4. Correlations between diversity of macroinvertebrates and environmental parameters Relations between environmental parameters and macroinvertebrates were more complex than with macrophytes, since numerous significant correlations were calculated (Table 6). Our results differed much from those published in Bird and Day (2016) who report that physical and chemical gradients did not correlate with species richness. Surface of the pond and T of the water, which do not reflect the quality of the pond, positively correlated with richness and diversity of macroinvertebrates. Positive correlation between surface area and richness and diversity of macroinvertebrates is in accordance with positive species-area relationship (MacArthur and Wilson, 1967). Moreover, surface area is a direct measure of potential available habitats in waterbodies (Triantis and Sfenthourakis, 2005). This result is interesting, since there was no such relation in case of macrophytes. A positive relationship between invertebrate richness and pond size was also found by Biggs et al. (2005), Studinski and Grubbs (2007), De Marco et al. (2014), whereas Boix et al. (2008), Hamerlik et al. (2014) found no relationship between them. Human pressure expressed as land use in the catchment and intensity of trampling of the banks by cattle negatively correlated with diversity of macroinvertebrates. Overgrazing by cattle causes eutrophication, physical destruction of the vegetation and disturbance (Bouahim et al., 2014), which can result in an impoverishment of the fauna. We also found out that the extent and intensity of trampling of the banks and/or littoral zone negatively correlated with diversity and richness of macroinvertebrates as well as macrophytes. Similarly Morrison and Bohlen (2010) report that intensive grazing lowers diversity and richness of aquatic invertebrates, since it lowers the complexity and biomass of vegetation and increase nutrient levels, which change macrophyte communities used by invertebrates (Steinman et al., 2003). Turbidity and contents of TP and nitrates which represent trophic status, negatively correlated with diversity of MI, meaning that lower quality of pond ecosystem causes a decrease in diversity and richness of its communities.
